intro: Braga's oldest tree is North American: a tulip tree of about 285 years in the baroque garden of the Palacio dos Biscainhos, now the city museum, and one of ten finalists for Portugal's Tree of the Year in 2026. Out at Santa Tecla, a cork oak and a group of three oaks share one square and were protected in the same act in 2012. At the foot of the Bom Jesus funicular, an oak and a plane both carry the same official name, the tree of the embrace.
meta_description: Braga's protected trees: a 285-year-old tulip tree at the Biscainhos museum, a cork oak and three oaks at Santa Tecla, and the Trees of the Embrace.
question_meta: Braga's oldest tree is the tulip tree in the Biscainhos garden, about 285 years old and a 2026 Tree of the Year finalist. Where it stands, plus three more.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Braga is the tulip tree in the garden of the Palacio dos Biscainhos, at roughly 285 years. That figure is solid by the standards of this page: Portugal's register of trees of public interest dated it to 270 years when it measured it in 2010, and newspaper coverage of its 2026 Tree of the Year nomination independently places the planting in the reign of Joao V, who died in 1750. Nothing else in the city is close. The cork oak at Santa Tecla is about 165 years old, the oak and plane at the Bom Jesus funicular around 115, and the three oaks sharing the Santa Tecla square around a century.
question_context: Every age on this page starts in the same place, Portugal's national register of trees of public interest, which records an age at the moment of measurement rather than a running figure. All four of these entries were classified in 2010 or 2011, so the years since have been added and the result rounded, which is why the numbers read as approximate. Where local reporting gives a different height or crown spread, as it does for the tulip tree, both figures are stated rather than reconciled. Two of the four entries cover more than one tree, because the register itself lists them that way: the three oaks of Santa Tecla are a single grouped classification, and the oak and plane at Bom Jesus share one registered name. All four are free to visit and none is gated, though the Biscainhos garden keeps museum hours and closes on Mondays. Two further classified trees stand in the walled grounds of the Mosteiro de Tibaes, which are closed to visitors while building works run.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Braga?
faq.a: The tulip tree in the garden of the Palacio dos Biscainhos, at around 285 years. The national register dated it to 270 years in 2010, and it was a finalist for Portugal's Tree of the Year in 2026.

faq.q: Are Braga's protected trees free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. The Biscainhos garden is free to enter, though it keeps museum hours and closes on Mondays; the palace's indoor exhibit is a separate ticket you do not need to see the tree. Santa Tecla and the Bom Jesus funicular station are open public ground at any hour.

faq.q: Why are two trees called the Trees of the Embrace?
faq.a: Both an oak and a plane at the Bom Jesus funicular station carry that name, arvore do Abraco, in their own official register entries, classified together in 2010. No source we have found explains where the name came from. If you know, tell us.

faq.q: Can I see them all in one walk?
faq.a: No. These are three separate stops. The Biscainhos garden is in the centre, Santa Tecla is about 1.5 kilometres east, roughly a 25 minute walk, and the Bom Jesus funicular is 5 kilometres out and served by city bus.

trees.name: The Tulip Tree of Biscainhos

location.address: Jardim do Palacio dos Biscainhos, Rua dos Biscainhos, Braga

trees.story:
Portugal shortlisted this tree for its Tree of the Year in 2026, one of ten finalists nationally. It is a tulip tree, Liriodendron tulipifera, native to the eastern United States, and the coverage of that shortlist calls it the largest of its kind in the country.

The measurements depend on who took them. Portugal's register of trees of public interest recorded 6.5 metres round the trunk, 27.4 metres tall and a crown of 18 metres when it classified the tree in 2010. The 2026 reporting gives 30 metres and 19. Both are plausible for a tree that has kept growing, and neither is picked here as the winner.

Age is firmer. The register put it at 270 years at that 2010 measurement, which makes it roughly 285 now, and the newspaper coverage places the planting in the reign of Joao V, who died in 1750. It went into the baroque garden of the Palacio dos Biscainhos, a hectare of formal beds, orchard and kitchen garden behind a Braga townhouse that is now the city's museum.

It was planted as one of a symmetrical pair. The other tulip tree lasted until the late 1970s; a replacement went in nearby in 1997 and is still an obviously young tree. The gap between the two is the clearest thing on the site for understanding what 285 years actually does.
trees.how_to_recognise: The very large one. A second, much smaller tulip tree stands nearby, planted in 1997 to replace the original's lost twin, and no visitor could mistake the two for the same age.
trees.access: Free. The Biscainhos museum garden is open Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00-12:30 and 14:00-17:30 (closed Mondays and some holidays); garden entry is free, just ask at reception. The palace's indoor exhibit is a separate paid ticket (EUR 2), not needed to see the tree.
trees.transport: Central Braga, an easy walk from the historic centre / cathedral.

trees.name: The Cork Oak of Santa Tecla

location.address: Largo de Santa Tecla, Calcada de Santa Tecla, Braga

trees.story:
The parish spent about six years asking before this cork oak was protected. When the classification came through they marked it on 21 March 2012, World Forest Day, with fourth-year pupils from the primary school up the road, who were handed the job of guarding it.

The national register gives the trunk 3.5 metres round, the tree 15 metres tall, and the crown 21 metres across, which is wider than the tree is high. That shape is the point of it. Largo de Santa Tecla is a square people actually use, and what a crown like that produces on a Minho summer afternoon is shade. The register dated the tree to 150 years at the 2011 measurement, so about 165 now.

Quercus suber is the tree the cork industry is built on, and Portugal produces more cork than any other country. The bark is the reason: thick, spongy, fire-resistant, and it grows back after stripping, which almost no other tree manages. A cork oak standing in a public square is generally left unharvested and keeps that bark, deeply furrowed and pale, a surface that looks several sizes too big for the trunk underneath.

Three oaks classified in the same act stand about sixty metres away, so the whole stop takes a minute.
trees.how_to_recognise: The tree with corky, deeply furrowed pale bark and evergreen leaves. The three oaks sixty metres away have smoother bark and drop their leaves in winter.
verified_sources: monumentaltrees.com (French-language record, girth and height match the register exactly, used only as corroboration per the site's rules, not as a source)
trees.access: Free. Stands in Largo de Santa Tecla, a public square used as a neighbourhood gathering space, open at all times.
trees.transport: About 1.5km from central Braga; a 20-25 minute walk, or a short bus/taxi ride.

trees.name: The Three Oaks of Santa Tecla

location.address: Largo de Santa Tecla, Calcada de Santa Tecla, Braga

trees.story:
Three oaks, one entry. Portugal's register of trees of public interest classifies these as a conjunto arboreo, a single grouped listing, and gives one set of figures for all three: 2.7 metres round, 16.7 metres tall, and 85 years old when they were measured in 2011, so around a century now. It does not say which of the three the tape went round, or whether the number is an average.

They stand in the same square as the cork oak, sixty metres off, and were protected in the same act, celebrated at the same ceremony on World Forest Day in March 2012. The local paper covering it described the oaks as one of the main attractions of Largo de Santa Tecla, valued for shade in summer and for the space underneath them, which the neighbourhood uses as its own.

Quercus robur is the common oak of northern Europe, and northern Portugal is near the warm edge of where it grows well. The name comes from the acorns: they hang on long stalks, peduncles, while the leaves sit almost directly on the twig, which is the reverse of the arrangement on a sessile oak and the quickest way to tell the two apart in autumn.
trees.how_to_recognise: The group of three deciduous oaks in the square, standing together about sixty metres from the single cork oak with the thick corky bark.
trees.access: Free. Same public square as the Cork Oak of Santa Tecla, open at all times.
trees.transport: About 1.5km from central Braga; a 20-25 minute walk, or a short bus/taxi ride.

best_time.label: August to September: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.name: The Trees of the Embrace
trees.species: Pedunculate Oak and London Plane (Quercus robur, Platanus x acerifolia)

location.address: Estacao do Elevador do Bom Jesus do Monte, Braga

trees.story:
An oak and a plane standing twenty metres apart at the foot of the Bom Jesus funicular are registered under the same name: arvore do Abraco, the tree of the embrace. That is not a nickname picked up from a guidebook. It is written into each tree's own entry in Portugal's register of trees of public interest, and both were classified on the same day in July 2010.

What nobody has written down is why. No source we have found explains the name: whether the two crowns once met over the path, whether it belongs to a story attached to the sanctuary on the hill above, or whether it is simply what people in Tenoes have always called them. If you know where the name comes from, tell us and it goes on the page.

Both trees were put at 100 years old when they were measured in 2010, which makes them around 115 now. The oak is the heavier of the two, 3.7 metres round with a crown almost 25 metres across; the plane is slimmer at 2.55 metres and marginally the taller at 26.

They stand at the station of the Elevador do Bom Jesus, the water-counterbalanced funicular that has hauled pilgrims up to the sanctuary since 1882. Looking at the trees costs nothing. The ride is a separate ticket.
trees.how_to_recognise: Two trees of different species, twenty metres apart by the funicular station. The heavier one with the wide spreading crown is the oak; the taller with mottled, flaking bark is the plane.
trees.access: Free. Standing at the funicular (Elevador do Bom Jesus) station, a public spot at the base of the Bom Jesus do Monte sanctuary hill, open at all times; the funicular itself is a separate paid ride up the hill and not needed to see the trees.
trees.transport: About 5km east of central Braga; city bus to Bom Jesus do Monte, then a short walk to the funicular station.

trees.name: The Turiz Oak

location.address: Rua do Pombal, Turiz, Vila Verde

verified_sources: https://www.icnf.pt/ (Arvoredo de Interesse Publico register, imported in data/registers/portugal-icnf.json)

official_register.name: ICNF Arvoredo de Interesse Publico, processo KNJ1/560 (Aviso n.o 15, 23/07/2010)

trees.access: Stands at a road junction in front of the Casa do Cruzeiro on Rua do Pombal; seen from the public road. View from the street, do not enter the house grounds.
trees.story:
Between 2010 and 2017 this oak grew six metres taller, at least on paper. Portugal's register of trees of public interest measured it at 21 metres when it classified the tree in 2010. The parish council of Turiz measured 27 metres in 2017. An oak this age does not put on six metres in seven years, so one of the two figures is off, and nobody has said which. The girth moved less: 4.18 metres in the register, 4.28 metres at chest height and 5.32 at the base in the parish's numbers.

The setting is the firmer part. It stands where two roads cross on Rua do Pombal, north of Braga in the municipality of Vila Verde, in front of the Casa do Cruzeiro, a house built in 1838 that the parish calls typical of an old Minho quinta. The register gave the oak 170 years in 2010 and the parish 180 in 2017, which lands its beginning close to the years the house went up. No source says the two were planned together, so read that as a coincidence of dates, not a story.

What you see from the road is the crown, about 23 metres by 22, nearly as wide as the tree is tall. The house is private, so this is a tree for the roadside.

The last published measurement is from 2017, and we have found no dated photograph since. If you pass it, tell us it still stands.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, about 23 metres across, spreading over a road junction. It stands on Rua do Pombal in front of the Casa do Cruzeiro, seen from the street.
trees.verify_notes: Register KNJ1/560: Quercus robur, Vila Verde, freguesia Turiz, lugar Casa do Cruzeiro, classified Aviso 15 of 23/07/2010, register age 170 (2010), girth 4.18 m, height 21 m, crown 22.3 m, coordinate 41.6262,-8.4544. Parish council page (Junta de Freguesia de Turiz, fetched): same tree, 'situated at the road crossing in front of the Casa do Cruzeiro, built 1838, typical of an old Minho quinta'; perimeter at base 5.32 m, at 1.30 m 4.28 m, crown 23.4 x 22.1 m, height 27.0 m, age 180 years, last measured 2017, address Rua do Pombal. Girth conflict stated: 4.18 m (2010 register) vs 4.28 m at 1.30 m (2017 parish); recorded 428. Height 21 m (2010) vs 27 m (2017). Nominatim confirms Rua do Pombal at the register coordinate (road node 41.62623,-8.45439). Alive: 2017 measurement is latest; lifecheck NONE, so flagged, no recent dated photo found. Pin is a register coordinate at a road junction, not confirmed on the crown (Overpass unreachable). Age is register-derived, at last measurement.

trees.story:
The owners of this tulip tree say it is 12 metres round. Portugal's register of trees of public interest says 5.94. Twelve would be an extraordinary waist for a tree of about 155 years, so the register's figure is the one used here, and the gap stays on the page. Height splits the same way: 25 metres on the owners' site, 36 in the register and in Wikipedia.

The family's own name for it is arvore do ponto, the tree of the point. None of our sources explains why.

It grows in the Mata de Pindela, the wood of a quinta near Vila Nova de Famalicao whose house, estate and wood are listed together as a Monumento de Interesse Publico. The register classified it in 2010 in the same notice as a coast redwood about 60 metres away and a Douglas fir a little further on. All three are North American, and the register put each at around 150 years when it measured them. Of the three, this is the one we know is alive: someone photographed it for iNaturalist on 30 October 2026.

Seeing it takes planning. Pindela is a private estate, now a hotel and events venue, and the owners open the gardens and wood only on guided visits booked in advance. It lies about 15 kilometres from Braga, roughly 5 beyond Famalicao, and no practical public transport reaches the gate. This is a booking and a car or taxi, not a detour on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, cut square across the tip, on a trunk about six metres round. It stands in the Mata de Pindela, about 60 metres from the estate's coast redwood.

best_time.label: October, when the square-tipped leaves turn clear yellow

Owner (Casa de Pindela) lists it as 'Tulipeiro-da-virginia (arvore do ponto)', 25 m high and 12 m perimeter; Wikipedia says about 36 m. Three registered trees in the mata stand within about 300 m (see brg_009, brg_010); the sequoia stands about 60 m from the tulip tree. Distance: about 15 km from Braga centre, roughly 5 km beyond Vila Nova de Famalicao; no practical public transport to the estate, a car or taxi trip (the 30-minute public transport rule is NOT met, say so). trees.story:
A redwood from the coast of California stands 40 metres tall in a wood near Vila Nova de Famalicao, and on this estate it is the one tree whose numbers everyone agrees on. Portugal's register of trees of public interest gives 40 metres in height and 5 metres round the trunk. The owners of the Quinta de Pindela say the same, and Wikipedia gives about 40 metres too. Next door, the tulip tree's girth is argued over by a factor of two.

The shape is a column. The register measured a crown only 12 metres across, so the tree is more than three times as tall as it is wide.

It was classified in 2010, in the same notice as the tulip tree about 60 metres away and a Douglas fir further into the Mata de Pindela, and the register put it at 150 years at that measurement. Nobody has recorded when it was planted or by whom. If you know, tell us.

We have no dated photograph of the redwood itself. The owners still name it as a tree worth visiting in their 2026 copy, and the tulip tree beside it was photographed alive in October 2026.

Pindela is a private estate, a hotel and events venue, and its wood opens only on guided visits booked in advance. It is about 15 kilometres from Braga with no practical public transport to the gate. Book once and see the redwood and the tulip tree as one stop.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, about 40 metres, on a narrow crown only 12 metres across and a trunk 5 metres round. It stands in the Mata de Pindela, about 60 metres from the estate's tulip tree.
trees.verify_notes: Register KNJ1/545: Sequoia sempervirens, Mata de Pindela, classified Aviso 4 of 10/03/2010, register age 150 (last measured 2010), girth 5 m, height 40 m, crown 12 m. Owner page: 'Sequoia, 40 metros de altura e 5 metros de perimetro', Wikipedia about 40 m; figures agree. Coast redwood planting is documented nowhere for this specimen; age is the register's, at 2010 measurement. Alive: lifecheck NONE for this coordinate (the nearby tulip tree has an iNaturalist observation 2026-10-30); owner site still names it as a visit-worthy tree in its 2026 copy. Flagged: register plus owner only, no dated photograph of the redwood itself. Same access and distance caveats as brg_008 (private estate, guided visit by booking, about 15 km from Braga, no public transport to the gate). About 60 m from the tulip tree (brg_008): the pair works as one stop.

trees.story:
Three sources agree this Douglas fir is 30 metres tall. They cannot agree how big round it is. Portugal's register of trees of public interest measured 4.5 metres when it classified the tree in 2010. The owners of the Quinta de Pindela give 6 metres. The register's figure is the one used here, and the difference stays on the page.

It is the third of the Mata de Pindela's protected trees, all North American, all classified in the same notice of March 2010. The coast redwood stands about 190 metres away and the tulip tree a little beyond it. Douglas fir comes from the Pacific side of North America, where it is one of the great timber trees, and this one was put at 150 years old at the 2010 measurement. Nobody has written down when it was planted.

The shape sets it apart from its redwood neighbour. Where the redwood's crown is 12 metres wide, the register measured this one at 20, on a tree of 30 metres.

The evidence that it still stands is thin: the owners still list it in their 2026 copy, but we have found no dated photograph. If you see it, tell us.

Pindela is a private estate, a hotel and events venue, and its wood opens only on guided visits booked in advance. It is about 15 kilometres from Braga, roughly 5 beyond Famalicao, with no practical public transport to the gate. Ask for all three trees on the same visit.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, about 20 metres across on a 30-metre tree, far broader than the redwood's 12. It stands in the Mata de Pindela, about 190 metres from that redwood.

Owner page says 30 m high and 6 m perimeter (girth conflict 4.5 vs 6 m, register kept); Wikipedia about 30 m. Alive: lifecheck NONE here; owner copy of 2026 still lists it. Flagged, register plus owner only. About 190 m from the redwood (brg_009). Same access and distance caveats as brg_008. Possibly better folded with brg_008/brg_009 as one visit; the writer decides.
